claim: Only two robustly replicated, genome-wide significant associations (near APOE and FOXO3) have been made to date for longevity.
source: As a result, only two robustly replicated, genome-wide significant associations (near APOE and FOXO3) have been made to date (Broer et al., 2015; Deelen et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies establishing these two loci.

claim: The study performed GWAS of survival in a sample of 1,012,240 parents (60% deceased) of European ancestry from UK Biobank and LifeGen.
source: We carried out GWAS of survival in a sample of 1,012,240 parents (60% deceased) of European ancestry from UK Biobank and a previously published meta-analysis of 26 additional population cohorts (LifeGen [Joshi et al., 2017]; Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the GWAS sample.

claim: The study performed a sex-stratified analysis and combined allelic effects in fathers and mothers into a single parental survival association in two ways.
source: We performed a sex-stratified analysis and then combined the allelic effects in fathers and mothers into a single parental survival association in two ways.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the analytical approach.

claim: The first analysis assumed genetic variants with common effect sizes (CES) for both parents.
source: First, we assumed genetic variants with common effect sizes (CES) for both parents, maximising power if the effect is indeed the same.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the CES analysis approach.

claim: The second analysis allowed for sex-specific effect sizes (SSE).
source: Second, we allowed for sex-specific effect sizes (SSE), maximising power to detect sexually dimorphic variants, including those only affecting one sex.
evidence: The Results section explicitly describes the SSE analysis approach.

claim: The study found 12 genomic regions with SNPs passing genome-wide significance.
source: We find 12 genomic regions with SNPs passing genome-wide significance for one or both analyses (p < 2.5 × 10–8, accounting for the two tests CES/SSE) (Figure 1; Table 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding, with reference to Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Five loci were discovered for the first time at or near MAGI3, KCNK3, HTT, HP, and LDLR.
source: Among these are five loci discovered here for the first time, at or near MAGI3, KCNK3, HTT, HP, and LDLR.
evidence: The Results section explicitly identifies these as novel discoveries.

claim: Carrying one copy of a life-extending allele is associated with an increase in lifespan between 0.23 and 1.07 years.
source: Carrying one copy of a life-extending allele is associated with an increase in lifespan between 0.23 and 1.07 years (around 3 to 13 months).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the effect size range.

claim: A variant had to have a minor allele frequency exceeding 5% and an effect size of 0.35 years of life or more per allele for the study to detect it with 80% power.
source: Despite our sample size exceeding 1 million phenotypes, a variant had to have a minor allele frequency exceeding 5% and an effect size of 0.35 years of life or more per allele for our study to detect it with 80% power.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the power calculation.

claim: The study found directionally consistent, nominally significant associations for six loci in LifeGen replication (p < 0.05, one-sided test).
source: Testing 20 candidate SNPs for which we had data available, we find directionally consistent, nominally significant associations for six loci (p < 0.05, one-sided test), of which three have sex-specific effects.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the replication findings.

claim: The study provides evidence against three putative loci but lacks statistical power to assess the remaining 11.
source: We also provide evidence against three putative loci but lack statistical power to assess the remaining 11 (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The study found directionally consistent evidence for SNPs near FOXO3 and EBF1 in longevity testing.
source: We then used our full sample to test six candidate SNPs previously associated with longevity (Zeng et al., 2016; Deelen et al., 2014; Flachsbart et al., 2009; Sebastiani et al., 2017) for association with lifespan, and find directionally consistent evidence for SNPs near FOXO3 and EBF1.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citations to previous studies.

claim: The remaining longevity SNPs did not associate with lifespan despite apparently adequate power.
source: The remaining SNPs did not associate with lifespan despite apparently adequate power to detect any effect similar to that originally reported (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The study found evidence d3-GHR does not associate with lifespan with any effect similar to that originally reported.
source: While this additive model reduces power relative to the correct model, our large sample size is more than able to offset the loss of power, and we find evidence d3-GHR does not associate with lifespan with any (recessive or additive) effect similar to that originally reported (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The integrated analysis reveals an additional seven genome-wide significant associations with lifespan.
source: The integrated analysis reveals an additional seven genome-wide significant associations with lifespan (Bayes Factor permutation p < 2.5 × 10–8), of which SNPs near TMEM18, GBX2/ASB18, IGF2R, POM12C, ZC3HC1, and ABO are reported at genome-wide significance for the first time (Figure 3; Table 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from iGWAS with reference to Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: A total of 82 independent SNPs associate with lifespan when allowing for a 1% false discovery rate (FDR).
source: A total of 82 independent SNPs associate with lifespan when allowing for a 1% false discovery rate (FDR) (Table 2—source data 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: All lead lifespan variants show directional consistency with the independent longevity sample.
source: Remarkably, all lead lifespan variants show directional consistency with the independent longevity sample, and 4 SNPs or close proxies (r2 > 0.8) reach nominal replication (p < 0.05, one-sided test) (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 4.

claim: SNPs near ABO, ZC3HC1, and IGF2R are replicated for the first time in longevity studies.
source: Of these, SNPs near ABO, ZC3HC1, and IGF2R are replicated for the first time, and thus appear to affect overall survival and survival to extreme age.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states these are novel replications.

claim: The overall ratio of replication effect sizes to discovery effect sizes – excluding APOE – is 0.42 (95% CI 0.23–0.61; p = 1.35 × 10−5).
source: The overall ratio of replication effect sizes to discovery effect sizes – excluding APOE – is 0.42 (95% CI 0.23–0.61; p = 1.35 × 10−5).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this statistical finding.

claim: Most lifespan SNPs are indeed longevity SNPs.
source: The fact this ratio is significantly greater than zero indicates most lifespan SNPs are indeed longevity SNPs.
evidence: The Results section explicitly interprets the statistical finding.

claim: Most lifespan SNPs may affect early mortality more than survival to extreme age, relative to APOE.
source: However, the fact most SNPs have a ratio smaller than one indicates they may affect early mortality more than survival to extreme age, relative to APOE (which itself has a greater effect on late-life mortality than early mortality) (Figure 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly interprets the statistical finding with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The study found 5 SNPs with differential effects on lifespan when stratified by sex and age (FDR 5%).
source: Although power was limited, as we sought contrasts in small effect sizes, we find 5 SNPs with differential effects on lifespan when stratified (FDR 5% across the 24 variants considered).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The effect of the APOE variant increases with age: the ε4 log hazard ratio on individuals older than 70 years is around 3 times greater than those between ages 40–70.
source: The effect of the APOE variant increases with age: the ε4 log hazard ratio on individuals older than 70 years is around 3 times greater than those between ages 40–70.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this age-specific finding.

claim: The effect of lead variants near CHRNA3/5, CDKN2B-AS1, and ABO tends to decline after age 60.
source: In contrast, the effect of lead variants near CHRNA3/5, CDKN2B-AS1, and ABO tends to decline after age 60, at least when expressed as hazard ratios (Figure 5A).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this age-specific finding with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Lead variants near APOE and PSORS1C3 show an effect (lnHR) of 0.036; 0.038 greater in women compared to men.
source: Independent of age, lead variants near APOE and PSORS1C3 also show an effect (lnHR) of 0.036; 0.038 greater in women (95% CI 0.013–0.059; 0.019–0.056, respectively), compared to men (Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this sex-specific finding with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: The SNP near ZW10 may affect men and women equally.
source: Notably, the SNP near ZW10, which was identified by Pilling et al. (2017) in fathers, and which replicated in LifeGen fathers, may affect men and women equally (95% CI years gained per effect allele, men 0.17–0.42, women 0.04–0.31), as measured in our meta-analysis of UK Biobank and LifeGen.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citation to Pilling et al. (2017).

claim: The study suggests causal roles for expression of PSRC1, SESN1, SH2B3, PSMA4, FURIN, FES, and KANK2 at 5% FDR using SMR-HEIDI.
source: Using blood eQTL summary statistics from two studies (Westra et al., 2013; Lloyd-Jones et al., 2017), we suggest causal roles for expression of PSRC1, SESN1, SH2B3, PSMA4, FURIN, FES, and KANK2 at 5% FDR (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citations to eQTL studies.

claim: GTEx tissue-wide expression data suggests further roles for 16 genes across 24 tissues.
source: GTEx tissue-wide expression data suggests further roles for 16 genes across 24 tissues, especially FES (nine tissues), PMS2P3 (six tissues) and PSORS1C1 (four tissues).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Methylation data reveals roles for 44 CpG sites near nine loci.
source: Methylation data reveals roles for 44 CpG sites near nine loci, especially near the PSORS1C3 locus (21 sites), APOE locus (nine sites), and HLA-DQA1 locus (four sites) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Conditional analysis identified an additional 335 variants associated with lifespan.
source: We find substantial allelic heterogeneity in several association intervals and identify an additional 335 variants, which increase out-of-sample explained variance from 0.095% to 0.169% (78% increase).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from conditional analysis.

claim: CELSR2/PSRC1, KCNK3, HLA-DQA1, LPA, ZW10, FURIN/FES, and APOE are amongst the most heterogeneous loci with at least 25 variants per locus showing independent effects.
source: CELSR2/PSRC1, KCNK3, HLA-DQA1, LPA, ZW10, FURIN/FES, and APOE are amongst the most heterogeneous loci with at least 25 variants per locus showing independent effects (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Alleles which increase lifespan associate with a reduction in cardiometabolic disease.
source: Under these restrictions, we find alleles which increase lifespan associate with a reduction in cardiometabolic, autoimmune, smoking-related, and neuropsychiatric disease and their disease risk factors (Table 1, Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Alleles which increase lifespan associate with a reduction in autoimmune disease.
source: Under these restrictions, we find alleles which increase lifespan associate with a reduction in cardiometabolic, autoimmune, smoking-related, and neuropsychiatric disease and their disease risk factors (Table 1, Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Alleles which increase lifespan associate with a reduction in smoking-related disease.

claim: Alleles which increase lifespan associate with a reduction in neuropsychiatric disease.

claim: None of the loci show any association with cancer other than lung cancer.
source: None of the loci show any association with cancer other than lung cancer.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The Alzheimer's disease locus APOE shows the largest lifespan variance explained (0.23 years2).
source: The Alzheimer's disease locus APOE shows the largest LVE (0.23 years2), consistent with its most frequent discovery as a lifespan SNP in GWAS (Joshi et al., 2016; Pilling et al., 2017; Deelen et al., 2014; Deelen et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with citations to previous studies.

claim: Of the 20 largest LVE SNPs, 12 associate with CVD.
source: Of the 20 largest LVE SNPs, 12 and 4 associate with CVD and smoking/lung cancer, respectively, while only two associate with other cancers (near ZW10 and NRG1; neither in the top 15 LVE SNPs).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Of the 20 largest LVE SNPs, 4 associate with smoking/lung cancer.
source: Of the 20 largest LVE SNPs, 12 and 4 associate with CVD and smoking/lung cancer, respectively, while only two associate with other cancers (near ZW10 and NRG1; neither in the top 15 LVE SNPs).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: Of the 20 largest LVE SNPs, only two associate with other cancers (near ZW10 and NRG1).
source: Of the 20 largest LVE SNPs, 12 and 4 associate with CVD and smoking/lung cancer, respectively, while only two associate with other cancers (near ZW10 and NRG1; neither in the top 15 LVE SNPs).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The top 20 LVE SNPs explain 0.33 years2 through CVD.
source: Cumulatively, the top 20/45 LVE SNPs explain 0.33/0.43 years2 through CVD, 0.13/0.15 years2 through smoking and lung cancer, and 0.03/0.11 years2 through other cancers (Figure 6).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The top 20 LVE SNPs explain 0.13 years2 through smoking and lung cancer.
source: Cumulatively, the top 20/45 LVE SNPs explain 0.33/0.43 years2 through CVD, 0.13/0.15 years2 through smoking and lung cancer, and 0.03/0.11 years2 through other cancers (Figure 6).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The top 20 LVE SNPs explain 0.03 years2 through other cancers.

evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Two of the three largest LVE loci for non-lung cancers (at or near ATXN2/BRAP and CDKN2B-AS1) show increased cancer protection associating with decreased lifespan due to antagonistic pleiotropy with CVD.
source: Strikingly, two of the three largest LVE loci for non-lung cancers (at or near ATXN2/BRAP and CDKN2B-AS1) show increased cancer protection associating with decreased lifespan (due to antagonistic pleiotropy with CVD)
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The disease loci included in the study with significant effects on lifespan explain 0.95 years2.
source: Together, the disease loci included in our study with significant effects on lifespan explain 0.95 years2, or less than 1% of the phenotypic variance of lifespan of European parents in UK Biobank (123 years2), and around 5% of the heritability.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: The disease loci explain less than 1% of the phenotypic variance of lifespan of European parents in UK Biobank.

claim: At an FDR < 5%, the study found enrichment in SNP heritability in five categories: two histone and two chromatin marks linked to male and female foetal brain cells, and one histone mark linked to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPC) of the brain.
source: At an FDR < 5%, we find enrichment in SNP heritability in five categories: two histone and two chromatin marks linked to male and female foetal brain cells, and one histone mark linked to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPC) of the brain.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from stratified LD-score regression.

claim: No other cell type categories are statistically significant after multiple testing correction.
source: Despite testing other cell types, such as heart, liver, and immune cells, no other categories are statistically significant after multiple testing correction (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: VEGAS highlights 33 gene sets at an FDR < 5%.
source: VEGAS highlights 33 gene sets at an FDR < 5%, but neither PASCAL nor DEPICT (with SNP thresholds at p < 5 × 10–8 and p < 1 × 10–5) identify any gene sets passing multiple testing correction.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from pathway analysis.

claim: Neither PASCAL nor DEPICT identify any gene sets passing multiple testing correction.
source: VEGAS highlights 33 gene sets at an FDR < 5%, but neither PASCAL nor DEPICT (with SNP thresholds at p < 5 × 10–8 and p < 1 × 10–5) identify any gene sets passing multiple testing correction.

claim: The 33 gene sets highlighted by VEGAS are principally for blood lipid metabolism (21).
source: The 33 gene sets highlighted by VEGAS are principally for blood lipid metabolism (21), with the majority involving lipoproteins (14) or homeostasis (4).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: eQTLs associated with lifespan are 1.69 to 3.39 times more likely to have age-dependent gene expression.
source: We find eQTLs associated with lifespan are 1.69 to 3.39 times more likely to have age-dependent gene expression, depending on the P value threshold used to define the set of lifespan SNPs (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding.

claim: An increase of one standard deviation in PRS increases lifespan by 0.8 to 1.1 years.
source: When including all independent markers, we find an increase of one standard deviation in PRS increases lifespan by 0.8 to 1.1 years, after doubling observed parent effect sizes to compensate for the imputation of their genotypes (see Table 3—source data 1 for a comparison of performance of different PRS thresholds).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from PRS analysis.

claim: The difference in median survival for the top and bottom deciles of PRS is 5.6/5.6 years for Scottish fathers/mothers.
source: Correspondingly – again after doubling for parental imputation – we find a difference in median survival for the top and bottom deciles of PRS of 5.6/5.6 years for Scottish fathers/mothers, 6.4/4.8 for English and Welsh fathers/mothers and 3.0/2.8 for Estonian fathers/mothers.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from PRS analysis.

claim: The difference in median survival for the top and bottom deciles of PRS is 6.4/4.8 years for English and Welsh fathers/mothers.

evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from PRS analysis.

claim: The difference in median survival for the top and bottom deciles of PRS is 3.0/2.8 years for Estonian fathers/mothers.
source: Correspondingly – again after doubling for parental imputation – we find a difference in median survival for the top and bottom deciles of PRS of 5.6/5.6 years for Scottish fathers/mothers, 6.4/4.8 for English and Welsh fathers/mothers and 3.0/2.8 for Estonian fathers/mothers.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from PRS analysis.

claim: In the Estonian Biobank, the contrast in survival for male/female subjects across the PRS tenth to first deciles is 3.5/2.7 years.
source: In the Estonian Biobank, where data is available for a wider range of subject ages (i.e. beyond median survival age) we find a contrast of 3.5/2.7 years in survival for male/female subjects, across the PRS tenth to first deciles (Table 3, Figure 8).
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Table 3 and Figure 8.

claim: A high PRS has a larger protective effect on lifespan for mothers than fathers in UK Biobank subsamples (p = 0.0071).
source: We find a high PRS has a larger protective effect on lifespan for mothers than fathers in UK Biobank subsamples (p = 0.0071), and has a larger protective effect on lifespan in younger age bands (p = 0.0001) (Figure 9)
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 9.

claim: A high PRS has a larger protective effect on lifespan in younger age bands (p = 0.0001).
source: We find a high PRS has a larger protective effect on lifespan for mothers than fathers in UK Biobank subsamples (p = 0.0071), and has a larger protective effect on lifespan in younger age bands (p = 0.0001) (Figure 9)
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding with reference to Figure 9.

claim: Higher PRS scores are associated with less heart disease.
source: We find that overall, higher PRS scores (i.e. genetically longer life) are associated with less heart disease, diabetes, hypertension, respiratory disease and lung cancer, but increased prevalence of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, prostate cancer and breast cancer, the last three primarily in parents.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states this finding from disease association analysis.

claim: The association of lifespan variants with well-known, life-shortening diseases is not surprising.
source: The association of lifespan variants with well-known, life-shortening diseases (cardiovascular, autoimmune, smoking-related diseases and lung cancer; Mathers et al., 2018) is not surprising, but the paucity of associations with other forms of cancer – without pleiotropic effects on CVD – is.
evidence: The Discussion section explicitly states this interpretation with citation.

claim: The paucity of associations with other forms of cancer (without pleiotropic effects on CVD) is surprising.
source: The association of lifespan variants with well-known, life-shortening diseases (cardiovascular, autoimmune, smoking-related diseases and lung cancer; Mathers et al., 2018) is not surprising, but the paucity of associations with other forms of cancer – without pleiotropic effects on CVD – is.

claim: Cancer deaths may often be due to rarer variants or environmental exposures.
source: This paucity suggests cancer deaths may often be due to (perhaps many) rarer variants or environmental exposures, although effect sizes might simply be slightly below our cut-off threshold to detect.

claim: The variants and pathways identified do not appear to underpin a generalised form of ageing independent of disease.
